Remember one distinction: delivery drivers get the goods to the customer; driver/sales workers deliver and complete the sale. One handles delivery, while the other combines delivery with business development.

This field does not suit people who dislike long driving hours, cannot tolerate lifting, avoid customer contact, or struggle with punctuality. Outdoor work brings heat, cold, and weather exposure. Delays and poor customer service create immediate problems.
A common path is: earn a driver's license → work as a delivery associate or driver assistant → drive a light truck independently → become a driver/sales worker or route supervisor.

This field suits people who learn routes quickly, handle physical work, prefer fieldwork, and relate well to customers. If on-time delivery and customer satisfaction define good work for you, this role offers stability.

Light Truck Drivers operate light vehicles for local or short-haul deliveries and follow optimized routes. Driver/sales workers also sell products, replenish stock, collect payments, and maintain customer relationships. The role connects warehouses with end customers.

paragraphs: Start at the station by collecting packages, checking the route, and loading the vehicle. Drive the route, unload goods, and confirm each delivery. Driver/sales workers visit regular customers to replenish stock and collect payments. Return to the station in the evening, reconcile payments and paperwork, refuel or charge the vehicle, and review the next day's route.
